610.title: Simhika
610.hook: flying fast over the sea, Hanuman suddenly slows down, and nothing seems to be holding him
610.howItsDone: In Sundara Kanda recitations, Simhika is remembered as the third of the beings Hanuman meets over the sea, and tellers often contrast her with Surasa, who tested him and blessed him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a Hanuman the size of a thumb, and Surasa's rule and his promise, both kept at once.

Hanuman is flying fast, Surasa's blessing behind him, the sea open ahead. He has met a mountain and a serpent mother out here, and both of them he could see. Then, all at once, his speed fails. He's being held back, Valmiki says, like a great ship against a contrary wind. No storm, no wall, no monster. Every stretch of air takes more effort than the last, and when he looks around, there's nothing there.
screen: `HIS SPEED FAILS.` → `LIKE A SHIP AGAINST THE WIND.` → `NOTHING THERE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman looks up, down, left, right. Then he looks below, at the water, and he sees her. A huge creature has risen from the sea: Simhika, a rakshasi, a demoness, who catches creatures by their shadows. She has seized Hanuman's shadow where it falls on the waves, and through it she is dragging him down. Hanuman knows what she is. Valmiki says he remembers: this is the shadow-catching creature Sugriva, the monkey king, told them about before the search began, when he briefed his searchers on the dangers of each direction. So the slowing wasn't weakness, and it wasn't his imagination. It had a name. Look at how the danger works. Simhika doesn't attack Hanuman. She attacks his shadow, the part of him down on the water that he isn't watching. Only when he stops looking ahead and looks down, at what's below and behind him, can he see what's been holding him back. And Simhika is different from Surasa. Surasa was sent by the gods to test him, and blessed him when he passed. Simhika is not a test. She simply wants to eat whatever flies over her water. She opens her mouth wide. And Hanuman, knowing exactly what he faces now, gets ready.
screen: `HANUMAN LOOKS ALL AROUND.` · `SHE HAS SEIZED HIS SHADOW.` · `SUGRIVA HAD WARNED THEM.` · then, large: `NOT A TEST THIS TIME.`

segments.voice: Think of something that's been slowing you down lately without a clear reason, and instead of pushing forward, do what Hanuman did: look down. Ask gently what's underneath it, tiredness, a worry, an old habit, something someone said. You don't have to fix it; just see if it has a name, and breathe with whatever you find.
Simhika. The rakshasi in the southern sea who catches flying creatures by their shadows, and drags Hanuman down until he looks below and recognizes her.
Your line: she has seized his shadow. Tomorrow, the far shore comes into view. That's day six hundred ten.

611.title: Simhika
611.hook: three meetings over the sea, three different answers, and then the far shore
611.howItsDone: Readers of the Sundara Kanda often point to the verse about steadiness, insight, intelligence and skill as a summary of Hanuman's character.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Simhika seized his shadow and dragged him down, until he looked below and knew her.

A good doctor doesn't treat every patient the same way. Knowing which response a moment needs is a skill all its own. Over one stretch of sea, Hanuman has now met three beings. One offered him rest. One tested him. And one, Simhika, wants to swallow him whole. Same monkey, same crossing, same water. Watch how differently he answers each.
screen: `WHICH RESPONSE DOES THIS NEED?` → `REST, A TEST, A THREAT.`

segments.voice: Simhika opens her mouth wide, and at first Hanuman does what worked with Surasa. He makes himself huge, and she opens wider. Then he makes himself small and drops straight into her mouth. But this time he doesn't dart back out with a bow. Inside her, Valmiki says, he tears at her vital organs with his nails, then shoots out again, quick as thought. Simhika falls dead into the sea. The beings watching from the sky cheer, and they give him a line worth keeping: whoever has, as you do, four things, steadiness, insight, intelligence and skill, does not fail at the work. Set the three meetings side by side. Mainaka offered a gift, and Hanuman answered with courtesy: a touch of the hand, a thank-you, and onward. Surasa set a test from the gods, and he answered with wit: smaller, not bigger, both promises kept. Simhika was simply a danger, and he answered with force, quickly and completely. Same Hanuman, three different responses. That's the four in action: steadiness to stay on course, insight to see what each thing really is, intelligence to choose the move, skill to carry it out. Then he looks ahead and sees it at last: the far shore. Trees, a line of hills, and beyond them a city. He comes down on a mountain at the water's edge, and Valmiki notes that after a hundred yojanas, he isn't even out of breath.
screen: `INTO THE MOUTH, AND OUT AGAIN.` · `STEADINESS, INSIGHT, MIND, SKILL.` · `COURTESY, WIT, FORCE.` · then, large: `THE FAR SHORE.`

segments.voice: Think back over yesterday and find three moments that asked something different of you: one that needed kindness, one cleverness, one firmness. For each, notice what you actually gave, with no grading. Then let the breath come and go, steady, as Hanuman lands without being out of breath.

612.title: Lanka by night
612.hook: the bravest monkey in the army looks at the golden city and decides to wait until dark, and to be the size of a cat
612.carry: a swan gliding on a lake
612.howItsDone: Storytellers telling the Sundara Kanda often dwell on Hanuman's careful reasoning before entering Lanka, and on his choice to go in small, by night.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Simhika, and four things, steadiness, insight, intelligence and skill, seen in three meetings answered with courtesy, wit and force.

Hanuman stands on a hilltop at the edge of the sea, and in front of him is Lanka. A city on a mountain, ringed with golden walls, moats full of water, guarded gates, towers that seem to touch the clouds. Banners. Gardens. It is breathtaking, and it is very obviously a fortress. The monkey who just crossed an ocean in one leap stands still and thinks.
screen: `A CITY ON A MOUNTAIN.` → `GOLDEN WALLS, GUARDED GATES.` → `HANUMAN STANDS STILL.`

segments.voice: What Hanuman thinks about isn't how strong he is. It's how easily he could ruin everything. Valmiki lets us hear his reasoning. Rakshasas guard this city everywhere. If I'm seen in my own form, there'll be a fight, and even if I win, Ravana will know Rama has found him, and Sita may be moved or harmed. A messenger who acts without thinking can wreck the very thing he was sent to do. So his plan is the opposite of a hero's entrance. He'll wait for night, make himself small, the size of a cat, Valmiki says, and slip in unseen. Then he'll search the whole city, house by house, until he finds her. So he waits. The sun goes down over Lanka. He shrinks and makes for the city, and just as he sets out, the moon rises. Valmiki gives it a picture: the moon in the sky like a swan gliding on a lake, its light falling on the city as if to help him. After the leap across the sea, the next heroic act is patience. Waiting for dark. Choosing to be small. Courage in the Sundara Kanda isn't only the jump; it's knowing when to go unnoticed, so the real work can be done.
screen: `HOW EASILY HE COULD RUIN IT.` · `WAIT FOR NIGHT; BE CAT-SIZED.` · `THE MOON RISES LIKE A SWAN.` · then, large: `THE NEXT HEROIC ACT IS PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: Let yourself grow still and imagine dusk falling, the light dimming and sounds softening. Make yourself small for a moment, not in a sad way, just quiet and light, the way Hanuman waits on the hill with nothing to prove. If you like, picture a moon rising slowly, giving just enough light to see by.
Lanka, Ravana's island city, which Hanuman enters only after sunset, shrunk to the size of a cat, as the moon rises like a swan gliding on a lake.
Your line: a swan gliding on a lake. Someone at the gate is about to notice him anyway. Until tomorrow.

613.title: Lanka by night
613.hook: the city itself steps out to stop Hanuman, and then, once he's inside, the enemy's capital turns out to be full of music
613.carry: do what you came to do
613.howItsDone: Readers of the Sundara Kanda often note how richly Valmiki describes Lanka, and the encounter with the city's guardian is a well-known episode in recitations and dance-dramas.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lanka. Hanuman waited for dark, made himself the size of a cat, and went in by moonlight.

A city at night is never one sound. It's a hundred small ones: someone practicing piano, a couple arguing, a party, a kid reading under a lamp. Before Hanuman can hear any of that in Lanka, though, he has to get past the gate. And at the gate, a figure steps out of the dark. She is huge and fierce, and she asks what a monkey is doing here.
screen: `A HUNDRED SMALL SOUNDS.` → `A FIGURE AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: She is Lanka herself, the city's guardian spirit, sometimes called Lankini. She blocks his way, mocks him, and strikes him. Hanuman hits back but holds himself in: Valmiki says he uses only his left fist, and not with full force, because she is a woman. Even so, she falls. And from the ground she says something extraordinary. Long ago Brahma, the creator, warned me: when a monkey overpowers you, know that the end of the rakshasas has come. So go in. Do what you came to do. Then Hanuman is inside, and Valmiki opens the city to us. It is no cartoon villain's lair. Hanuman passes mansions bright with lamps. He hears singing and instruments, and from some houses, the Vedas being chanted. He sees lovers, people drinking, warriors with their weapons, guards on their rounds, rakshasas who are graceful and rakshasas who are frightening. Valmiki describes it with real admiration: Ravana's Lanka is wealthy, beautiful, learned and alive. Here the epic doesn't pretend the other side is ugly or empty. The city that holds Sita captive is full of music, prayer and ordinary lives. That makes Ravana's wrong sharper, not softer. And it makes Hanuman's task harder: somewhere in all this light and noise, one woman is grieving, and he has to find her unseen.
screen: `LANKA HERSELF AT THE GATE.` · `HE STRIKES WITH HIS LEFT FIST.` · `BRAHMA'S OLD WARNING.` · then, large: `A CITY FULL OF MUSIC AND PRAYER.`

614.title: Ravana's palace
614.hook: in the most splendid room in Lanka, Hanuman sees a beautiful queen asleep and thinks, for one wild moment, that his search is over
614.carry: he knew her character before he knew her face
614.howItsDone: Readers of the Sundara Kanda often smile at Hanuman's leap of joy over Mandodari, and commentators point to how he recognizes his mistake by reasoning about Sita's character.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rakshasa. The city's guardian fell and let him in, and inside, a capital full of music and prayer.

All night Hanuman has searched Lanka house by house, and every house has been the wrong one. Now he reaches the heart of the city, Ravana's own palace, glittering and guarded, and slips inside. In the innermost room he sees a woman so beautiful and regal that his heart leaps. After a hundred yojanas of sea and a city full of strangers, he's sure he has found her. He's about to celebrate too soon.
screen: `HOUSE BY HOUSE, ALL NIGHT.` → `THE INNERMOST ROOM.` → `HE'S SURE.`

segments.voice: Valmiki takes his time getting there. First Hanuman sees the Pushpaka, the flying chariot made by the divine craftsman Vishvakarma, which Ravana took from his half-brother Kubera. It's covered in jewels and seems to float. Then a vast hall where Ravana's many wives lie asleep after a night of music and wine, ornaments scattered, like a lake of lotuses closed for the night. Then Ravana himself, asleep on a magnificent bed, enormous and powerful. And near him, on a separate couch, a woman lovelier than all the rest, adorned and serene. Hanuman's joy explodes. He slaps his arms, kisses his tail, runs about, sings, climbs the pillars and jumps down again. He's a monkey, and for one moment he acts like one. Then he stops, and thinks. Sita, separated from Rama, would not sleep peacefully. She wouldn't wear jewels, or eat and drink at a banquet. She would never lie content in another man's palace. This is not Sita. The woman is Mandodari, Ravana's chief queen. It's a funny scene, and a telling one. He had only glimpsed Sita once, far off in the sky, as Ravana carried her past Sugriva's mountain. So he corrects his mistake not by looking harder at a face, but by thinking about who Sita is: her grief, her faithfulness, her love for Rama. He knew her character before he knew her face.
screen: `THE PUSHPAKA, THE FLYING CHARIOT.` · `A HALL OF SLEEPING QUEENS.` · `HANUMAN'S WILD JOY.` · then, large: `SITA WOULD NOT SLEEP LIKE THIS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you love, and instead of picturing their face, think of how they are: the way they laugh, what they'd do when sad, what they'd never do. Let those qualities come one at a time with each breath. You'd know them by these even in a crowd, even with your eyes closed.

615.title: Ravana's palace
615.hook: having searched every room, Hanuman sits down in the dark and considers giving up, and then talks himself back up
615.howItsDone: Some who recite the Sundara Kanda in hard times dwell on Hanuman's despair and recovery here, and on the phrase anirvedaḥ śriyo mūlam, 'not despairing is the root of good fortune'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana's palace, the flying chariot, the sleeping queens, and Mandodari, mistaken for Sita for one joyful moment.

Hanuman has searched Ravana's palace from end to end, room after room, and he hasn't found her. The night is wearing on. He has reached the end of the list, and he sits down. Sometimes the hardest moment isn't the danger; it's that. And Valmiki gives the hero of the Sundara Kanda something surprising here: a full, honest spell of despair.
screen: `THE END OF THE LIST.` → `HANUMAN SITS DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, a moment of conscience. Hanuman has walked among sleeping women, other men's wives, and looked at them. Has he done wrong? He thinks it through. His mind, he decides, was not disturbed: a woman must be searched for among women, and his intention was pure. Valmiki lets him weigh it rather than skip it. Then the despair. Maybe Sita is dead, he thinks. Maybe the rakshasas killed her. Early in it, Valmiki gives him a line in Sanskrit: anirvedaḥ śriyo mūlam. Not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune. He searches again, cellars, halls, corners. Still nothing. The despair comes back, deeper. If I go back without news, Rama will die of grief, then Lakshmana, then Bharata, then Rama's mothers, and on through Sugriva. He follows the chain of sorrow all the way down. For a while he even thinks of not going back at all, of staying by the sea as a hermit. Then, slowly, he turns. He bows in his heart to Rama and Lakshmana, to Sita, and to the gods, and begins again. The line didn't settle it once and for all. He said it, and still fell further. It's about what he did next, each time. Despair came and sat with him, and he didn't let it make the decision. This part ends with him looking out from the palace walls at a grove of trees he hasn't entered yet.
screen: `A MOMENT OF CONSCIENCE.` · `THE CHAIN OF SORROW.` · `ANIRVEDAH SHRIYO MULAM.` · then, large: `HE GETS UP AND SEARCHES AGAIN.`

segments.voice: If there's something you've been close to giving up on, let it come to mind gently, and don't argue with the discouragement; let it sit beside you, the way Hanuman's despair sat with him. Breathe with it. Then, on one breath, notice whether there's one place you haven't looked yet, one small next step, and just let it appear.

chat.says: Did Hanuman ever feel like giving up during his search?
options: Yes, deeply, but he chose not to let despair decide, and searched again.
No. A hero like him never doubts, so he simply kept on searching.
Yes, and he flew home to Rama without finding any news.
chat.meaning: Hanuman despaired more than once, but each time got up and searched again. Not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune.

616.title: the ashoka grove
616.hook: the grove's name means without sorrow, and in the middle of it sits the saddest person in Lanka
616.howItsDone: Sita in the Ashoka grove is a familiar scene in Ramayana painting and performance, and some devotees, reciting this part of the Sundara Kanda, slow down at the moment Hanuman first sees her.

segments.voice: Yesterday: every room searched, despair, and then the line: not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune.

Hanuman leaps over a garden wall beside Ravana's palace, into birdsong, streams and shade. It's a whole grove of ashoka, a South Asian tree that flowers red and orange, planted for its beauty. In Sanskrit the name means without sorrow: a, not, and shoka, sorrow. It's Ravana's pleasure garden. And Hanuman is about to find a name that says the opposite of what it holds.
screen: `OVER THE GARDEN WALL.` → `ASHOKA: WITHOUT SORROW.` → `A NAME AND ITS OPPOSITE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman climbs a tall shimshapa tree, thick with leaves, near a clear pool. If Sita is here, he reasons, she'll come to this water for her prayers at dawn. So he hides in the branches and watches. And then he sees her. Valmiki describes her slowly, the way you'd describe someone you'd waited a long time to see. She is thin from fasting. She wears a single faded garment. She sits on the ground, sighing, surrounded by rakshasis with fierce faces. Valmiki gives two pictures: a flame veiled in smoke, and a thin crescent moon behind clouds. The light is still there; it's just covered. How does Hanuman know it's her? Not from her face, which he had only glimpsed far off in the sky. From her ornaments: the ones she wears match those Rama described, and the ones missing are the ones she dropped on the mountain as Ravana carried her away. And from her grief, exactly what he reasoned Sita's would be, back in the palace. Valmiki says Hanuman weeps, there in the tree. So a long week ends. It began with Simhika catching his shadow over the sea, and Hanuman landing not out of breath. Then Lanka by night: the guardian at the gate, the city of music and prayer. Then the palace: the flying chariot, Mandodari mistaken for Sita, every room searched, despair and recovery. And now, in the grove called without sorrow, sorrow itself, sitting on the ground. Found.
screen: `UP THE SHIMSHAPA TREE.` · `A FLAME VEILED IN SMOKE.` · `KNOWN BY HER ORNAMENTS AND GRIEF.` · then, large: `HANUMAN WEEPS IN THE TREE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who seems fine on the outside but may be carrying something heavy, a light veiled in smoke, without needing the details. Hold them quietly in mind, the way Hanuman watches from the branches without intruding. Breathe in for them, breathe out for them, and let your care be steady and unhurried.
Ashoka, the tree whose name means without sorrow, and Ravana's grove of them, where Hanuman, hidden in a shimshapa tree, finally sees Sita, and weeps.
Your line: a flame veiled in smoke. She doesn't know yet that help is in the tree. That's day six hundred sixteen.

chat.says: How did Hanuman know the woman in the grove was really Sita?
